claim: Pharmacological studies in mammals suggest that norepinephrine (NE) plays an important role in promoting arousal.
source: Pharmacological studies in mammals suggest that norepinephrine (NE) plays an important role in promoting arousal.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature, as indicated by the context of the abstract.

claim: The role of endogenous NE is unclear, with contradicting reports concerning the sleep phenotypes of mice lacking NE due to mutation of dopamine β-hydroxylase (dbh).
source: However, the role of endogenous NE is unclear, with contradicting reports concerning the sleep phenotypes of mice lacking NE due to mutation of dopamine β-hydroxylase (dbh).
evidence: This claim references contradicting reports in the literature about dbh mutant mice.

claim: dbh mutant zebrafish exhibit dramatically increased sleep.
source: In contrast to mice, these animals exhibit dramatically increased sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 2).

claim: dbh mutant zebrafish have a reduced arousal threshold despite an increase in sleep.
source: Surprisingly, despite an increase in sleep, dbh mutant zebrafish have a reduced arousal threshold.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from arousal threshold assays (Figure 3).

claim: NE is important for Hcrt-induced arousal.
source: Using genetic overexpression of hypocretin (Hcrt) and optogenetic activation of hcrt-expressing neurons, we also find that NE is important for Hcrt-induced arousal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Hcrt overexpression and optogenetic experiments (Figures 4, 5, 8).

claim: NE is a critical downstream effector of Hcrt neurons.
source: These results establish a role for endogenous NE in promoting arousal and indicate that NE is a critical downstream effector of Hcrt neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing that NE is required for Hcrt-induced arousal.

claim: Neuronal centers that regulate sleep and wakefulness lie predominantly in the hypothalamus and brainstem.
source: Several studies have shown that neuronal centers that regulate sleep and wakefulness lie predominantly in the hypothalamus and brainstem (Pace-Schott and Hobson, 2002; Saper et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: NE has been implicated in many aspects of physiology and behavior, including cognition, attention, reward, locomotion and arousal.
source: Norepinephrine (NE) is one of the most abundant neurotransmitters in the central and peripheral nervous systems, and has been implicated in many aspects of physiology and behavior, including cognition, attention, reward, locomotion and arousal (Berridge and Waterhouse, 2003; Weinshenker and Schroeder, 2007; Sara, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Small molecule activators of NE signaling have been shown to increase wakefulness.
source: Small molecule activators of NE signaling have been shown to increase wakefulness, whereas inhibitors promote sleep (Berridge et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Small molecule inhibitors of NE signaling promote sleep.
source: Small molecule activators of NE signaling have been shown to increase wakefulness, whereas inhibitors promote sleep (Berridge et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: There are contradicting reports concerning the sleep phenotype of mice that do not synthesize NE due to mutation of dopamine beta hydroxylase (dbh).
source: However, the role of endogenous NE in regulating the sleep/wake cycles of vertebrates remains unclear, with contradicting reports concerning the sleep phenotype of mice that do not synthesize NE due to mutation of dopamine beta hydroxylase (dbh) (Hunsley and Palmiter, 2003; Ouyang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two studies with contradicting results.

claim: The locus coeruleus (LC) in the brainstem is a major arousal promoting center and a major source of NE in the brain.
source: The locus coeruleus (LC) in the brainstem is a major arousal promoting center and a major source of NE in the brain (reviewed in Berridge and Waterhouse, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Activation of the LC promotes sleep-to-wake transitions in mice.
source: Optogenetic studies in mice have shown that activation of the LC promotes sleep-to-wake transitions, while inhibition of the LC reduces time spent awake (Carter et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to optogenetic studies in mice.

claim: Inhibition of the LC reduces time spent awake in mice.
source: Optogenetic studies in mice have shown that activation of the LC promotes sleep-to-wake transitions, while inhibition of the LC reduces time spent awake (Carter et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to optogenetic studies in mice.

claim: Activation of the LC plays an important role in mediating the arousing effects of hypocretin (hcrt)-expressing neurons.
source: These studies also showed that activation of the LC plays an important role in mediating the arousing effects of hypocretin (hcrt)-expressing neurons (Carter et al., 2010, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to optogenetic studies in mice.

claim: Hcrt-expressing neurons constitute an important arousal center in the hypothalamus.
source: These studies also showed that activation of the LC plays an important role in mediating the arousing effects of hypocretin (hcrt)-expressing neurons (Carter et al., 2010, 2012), which constitute an important arousal center in the hypothalamus (Sutcliffe and de Lecea, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The LC produces dopamine, neuropeptide Y, neurotensin, and vasopressin in addition to NE.
source: However, in addition to NE, the LC also produces other neurotransmitters and neuropeptides that affect sleep, including dopamine (Dzirasa et al., 2006), neuropeptide Y (Dyzma et al., 2010), neurotensin (Erwin and Radcliffe, 1993) and vasopressin (Born et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Dopamine affects sleep.
source: However, in addition to NE, the LC also produces other neurotransmitters and neuropeptides that affect sleep, including dopamine (Dzirasa et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Neuropeptide Y affects sleep.
source: However, in addition to NE, the LC also produces other neurotransmitters and neuropeptides that affect sleep, including dopamine (Dzirasa et al., 2006), neuropeptide Y (Dyzma et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Neurotensin affects sleep.
source: However, in addition to NE, the LC also produces other neurotransmitters and neuropeptides that affect sleep, including dopamine (Dzirasa et al., 2006), neuropeptide Y (Dyzma et al., 2010), neurotensin (Erwin and Radcliffe, 1993)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Vasopressin affects sleep.
source: However, in addition to NE, the LC also produces other neurotransmitters and neuropeptides that affect sleep, including dopamine (Dzirasa et al., 2006), neuropeptide Y (Dyzma et al., 2010), neurotensin (Erwin and Radcliffe, 1993) and vasopressin (Born et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Zebrafish dbh mutants develop normally and are viable.
source: Contrary to dbh null mice (Thomas et al., 1995), zebrafish dbh mutants develop normally and are viable.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of the dbh mutant zebrafish.

claim: Murine dbh knockout displays no overt developmental defects.
source: Although the murine dbh knockout (Thomas et al., 1995) displays no overt developmental defects, only 10% of dbh−/− pups produced by dbh+/− mothers survive embryonic development and no dbh−/− pups are born to dbh−/− mothers
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Only 10% of dbh−/− pups produced by dbh+/− mothers survive embryonic development in mice.
source: Although the murine dbh knockout (Thomas et al., 1995) displays no overt developmental defects, only 10% of dbh−/− pups produced by dbh+/− mothers survive embryonic development and no dbh−/− pups are born to dbh−/− mothers
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: No dbh−/− pups are born to dbh−/− mothers in mice.
source: Although the murine dbh knockout (Thomas et al., 1995) displays no overt developmental defects, only 10% of dbh−/− pups produced by dbh+/− mothers survive embryonic development and no dbh−/− pups are born to dbh−/− mothers
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Female dbh−/− zebrafish produced a normal number of dbh−/− larvae when mated to dbh+/− males.
source: In contrast to the mouse knockout, female dbh−/− zebrafish produced a normal number of dbh−/− larvae when mated to dbh+/− males (out of 287 larvae genotyped from 3 independent crosses, 49% were dbh+/− and 51% were dbh−/−).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genotyping crosses.

claim: dbh−/− larvae completely lack NE.
source: We verified that dbh−/− larvae completely lack NE using an ELISA assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from an ELISA assay shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The level of dbh mRNA in dbh−/− larvae is much lower than in their dbh+/− siblings.
source: Using in situ hybridization (ISH) we also found that the level of dbh mRNA in dbh−/− larvae is much lower than in their dbh+/− siblings, presumably due to nonsense mediated decay of the mutant transcript (Isken and Maquat, 2007) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Only 40% of dbh mutant mice that survive embryogenesis reach adulthood.
source: While only 40% of dbh mutant mice that survive embryogenesis reach adulthood (Thomas et al., 1995), dbh−/− zebrafish embryos developed to adulthood normally (24/96 (25%) of embryos produced by a male dbh+/− crossed to female dbh+/−, and raised to adulthood, were identified as dbh−/−).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: dbh−/− zebrafish embryos developed to adulthood normally.
source: While only 40% of dbh mutant mice that survive embryogenesis reach adulthood (Thomas et al., 1995), dbh−/− zebrafish embryos developed to adulthood normally (24/96 (25%) of embryos produced by a male dbh+/− crossed to female dbh+/−, and raised to adulthood, were identified as dbh−/−).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that 25% of embryos from a dbh+/− cross reached adulthood as dbh−/−, which is the expected Mendelian ratio.

claim: dbh−/− larvae display lower overall activity during both day and night than sibling controls.
source: We observed that dbh mutants display lower overall activity (Figure 2A,D) and activity when awake (Figure 2B,E) during both day and night.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,D.

claim: dbh−/− larvae display lower activity when awake during both day and night than sibling controls.
source: We observed that dbh mutants display lower overall activity (Figure 2A,D) and activity when awake (Figure 2B,E) during both day and night.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,E.

claim: dbh−/− larvae sleep much more during both day (+185%) and night (+57%) than sibling controls.
source: Importantly, we found that dbh−/− larvae sleep much more during both day (+185%) and night (+57%) than sibling controls (Figure 2C,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,F.

claim: During the day, the increase in sleep in dbh−/− larvae was due solely to more frequent sleep bouts (+220%).
source: During the day, the increase in sleep was due solely to more frequent sleep bouts (+220%), while during the night both longer (+17%) and more frequent (+25%) sleep bouts occurred (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: During the night, the increase in sleep in dbh−/− larvae was due to both longer (+17%) and more frequent (+25%) sleep bouts.
source: During the day, the increase in sleep was due solely to more frequent sleep bouts (+220%), while during the night both longer (+17%) and more frequent (+25%) sleep bouts occurred (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: Sleep latency at night in dbh−/− larvae was reduced by 40%.
source: Furthermore, sleep latency at night in the mutants was reduced by 40% (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Treatment of dbh mutants with 100 μM prazosin did not affect sleep/wake behavior compared to DMSO controls.
source: It is interesting to note that, as expected, treatment of dbh mutants with 100 μM prazosin did not affect sleep/wake behavior compared to DMSO controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that prazosin-induced behavioral effects are specific to NE signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Prazosin-induced behavioral effects are specific to NE signaling.
source: It is interesting to note that, as expected, treatment of dbh mutants with 100 μM prazosin did not affect sleep/wake behavior compared to DMSO controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that prazosin-induced behavioral effects are specific to NE signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that prazosin has no effect in dbh mutants that lack NE.

claim: The ETP50 for dbh−/− larvae was 2.1 compared to 3.1 for their dbh+/+ siblings (32% decrease).
source: Surprisingly, the ETP50 for dbh−/− larvae was 2.1 compared to 3.1 for their dbh+/+ siblings (32% decrease) (p < 0.0001 by extra sum-of-squares F test)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from arousal threshold assays.

claim: dbh−/− larvae exhibited an increased maximal response fraction, from 0.43 for dbh−/− compared to 0.34 for dbh+/+.
source: In addition to a lower ETP50, dbh−/− larvae also exhibited an increased maximal response fraction, from 0.43 for dbh−/− compared to 0.34 for dbh+/+ (p < 0.0001 by extra sum-of-squares F test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from arousal threshold assays.

claim: Treatment with the alpha1-adrenergic antagonist prazosin or the alpha2-adrenergic agonist clonidine did not affect the arousal threshold of zebrafish larvae.
source: Interestingly, treatment with the alpha1-adrenergic antagonist prazosin or the alpha2-adrenergic agonist clonidine did not affect the arousal threshold of zebrafish larvae (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data that is mentioned but not shown.

claim: Larvae treated with the alpha2-adrenergic antagonist bopindolol showed a 54% decrease in their ETP50 from 5.7 to 2.6.
source: However, larvae treated with the alpha2-adrenergic antagonist bopindolol showed a 54% decrease in their ETP50 from 5.7 to 2.6 (Figure 3B, p < 0.0001 by extra sum-of-squares F test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Hcrt has been shown to promote wakefulness and inhibit sleep in zebrafish larvae.
source: The Hcrt neuropeptide has been shown to promote wakefulness and inhibit sleep in zebrafish larvae (Prober et al., 2006) and mammals (reviewed in Alexandre et al., 2013; Sakurai, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Hcrt has been shown to promote wakefulness and inhibit sleep in mammals.
source: The Hcrt neuropeptide has been shown to promote wakefulness and inhibit sleep in zebrafish larvae (Prober et al., 2006) and mammals (reviewed in Alexandre et al., 2013; Sakurai, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Stimulation of Hcrt neurons has been shown to promote sleep to wake transitions in mice.
source: The Hcrt neuropeptide has been shown to promote wakefulness and inhibit sleep in zebrafish larvae (Prober et al., 2006) and mammals (reviewed in Alexandre et al., 2013; Sakurai, 2013), and stimulation of Hcrt neurons has been shown to promote sleep to wake transitions in mice (Adamantidis et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The LC is densely innervated by Hcrt neurons in both zebrafish and mammals.
source: First, the LC is densely innervated by Hcrt neurons in both zebrafish (Prober et al., 2006) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B) and mammals (Peyron et al., 1998; Chemelli et al., 1999; Date et al., 1999; Horvath et al., 1999)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: LC neurons express the Hcrt receptor.
source: First, the LC is densely innervated by Hcrt neurons in both zebrafish (Prober et al., 2006) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B) and mammals (Peyron et al., 1998; Chemelli et al., 1999; Date et al., 1999; Horvath et al., 1999) and LC neurons express the Hcrt receptor (Horvath et al., 1999; Bourgin et al., 2000; Prober et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The medulla oblongata is another source of NE in the brain.
source: It is worth noting, however, that the medulla oblongata is another source of NE in the brain, and it also receives Hcrt projections in zebrafish (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and mammals (Ciriello et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The medulla oblongata receives Hcrt projections in zebrafish and mammals.
source: It is worth noting, however, that the medulla oblongata is another source of NE in the brain, and it also receives Hcrt projections in zebrafish (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and mammals (Ciriello et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Application of Hcrt peptide depolarizes LC neurons in brain slices.
source: Second, application of Hcrt peptide depolarizes LC neurons in brain slices (Hagan et al., 1999) and in vivo (Bourgin et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Application of Hcrt peptide depolarizes LC neurons in vivo.
source: Second, application of Hcrt peptide depolarizes LC neurons in brain slices (Hagan et al., 1999) and in vivo (Bourgin et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Acute inhibition of LC neurons using halorhodopsin inhibits the arousing effects of stimulating Hcrt neurons.
source: Third, acute inhibition of LC neurons using halorhodopsin inhibits the arousing effects of stimulating Hcrt neurons (Carter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The mammalian genome contains two hcrt receptor (hcrtr) paralogs, both of which are required for the increase in locomotor activity and decrease in sleep observed after injection of Hcrt peptide.
source: The mammalian genome contains two hcrt receptor (hcrtr) paralogs, both of which are required for the increase in locomotor activity and decrease in sleep observed after injection of Hcrt peptide (reviewed in Alexandre et al., 2013; Sakurai, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Hcrt protein levels remain elevated for over 48 hr after HS, with no detectable decrease during the first 24 hr after HS.
source: We previously showed that Hcrt protein levels remain elevated for over 48 hr after HS, with no detectable decrease during the first 24 hr after HS (Prober et al., 2006), so overexpressed Hcrt protein should remain at high levels throughout the night following HS.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: hcrtr+/− and hcrtr−/− larvae reacted similarly to the HS, with no significant difference in the amount of sleep between the two genotypes.
source: hcrtr+/− and hcrtr−/− larvae reacted similarly to the HS, with no significant difference in the amount of sleep between the two genotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Hcrt overexpression decreased the sleep of Tg(hsp:Hcrt);hcrtr+/− larvae by 50%.
source: Hcrt overexpression decreased the sleep of Tg(hsp:Hcrt);hcrtr+/− larvae by 50% (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D), as previously described for Tg(hsp:Hcrt);hcrtr+/+ larvae (Prober et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D and a citation to prior work.

claim: No decrease in sleep was observed in Tg(hsp:Hcrt);hcrtr−/− larvae following HS.
source: However, no decrease in sleep was observed in Tg(hsp:Hcrt);hcrtr−/− larvae following HS (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: The decrease in sleep following overexpression of Hcrt requires a functional hcrtr.
source: These results indicate that the decrease in sleep following overexpression of Hcrt requires a functional hcrtr.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that Hcrt overexpression does not decrease sleep in hcrtr−/− larvae.

claim: Larvae lacking the hsp:Hcrt transgene were similarly affected by the HS independently of whether they produced NE or not.
source: Larvae lacking the hsp:Hcrt transgene were similarly affected by the HS independently of whether they produced NE or not (no significant difference observed between dbh+/− and dbh−/− larvae, Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Lack of NE does not affect the response of larvae to HS.
source: We therefore conclude that lack of NE does not affect the response of larvae to HS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that dbh+/− and dbh−/− larvae respond similarly to HS.

claim: The sleep of Tg(hsp:Hcrt)+/−;dbh+/− larvae was reduced to 40% of the pre-HS value.
source: Specifically, the sleep of Tg(hsp:Hcrt)+/−;dbh+/− larvae was reduced to 40% of the pre-HS value (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The sleep of Tg(hsp:Hcrt)+/−;dbh−/− larvae was reduced to 75% of the pre-HS value.
source: However, the sleep of Tg(hsp:Hcrt)+/−;dbh−/− larvae was reduced to 75% of the pre-HS value (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The majority of Hcrt-induced sleep loss is blocked in the absence of NE.
source: Thus, the majority of Hcrt-induced sleep loss is blocked in the absence of NE.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of sleep reduction in dbh+/− and dbh−/− larvae after Hcrt overexpression.

claim: Treatment of Tg(hsp:Hcrt)+/− animals with prazosin similarly inhibits Hcrt overexpression-induced arousal.
source: Importantly, treatment of Tg(hsp:Hcrt)+/− animals with prazosin similarly inhibits Hcrt overexpression-induced arousal (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) suggesting that the dbh mutant phenotype is indeed due to the blocking of noradrenergic signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The dbh mutant phenotype is due to the blocking of noradrenergic signaling.
source: Importantly, treatment of Tg(hsp:Hcrt)+/− animals with prazosin similarly inhibits Hcrt overexpression-induced arousal (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) suggesting that the dbh mutant phenotype is indeed due to the blocking of noradrenergic signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that prazosin treatment phenocopies the dbh mutant.

claim: NE plays an important role in Hcrt-mediated arousal.
source: These results indicate that NE plays an important role in Hcrt-mediated arousal, but suggest that Hcrt also inhibits sleep via NE-independent mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that NE is required for most, but not all, of Hcrt-induced arousal.

claim: Hcrt also inhibits sleep via NE-independent mechanisms.
source: These results indicate that NE plays an important role in Hcrt-mediated arousal, but suggest that Hcrt also inhibits sleep via NE-independent mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that some Hcrt-induced arousal remains in the absence of NE.

claim: ChR2-EYFP is exclusively expressed in Hcrt neurons in Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP) larvae.
source: Using immunofluorescence, we verified that ChR2-EYFP is exclusively expressed in Hcrt neurons, and that all Hcrt neurons express ChR2-EYFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All Hcrt neurons express ChR2-EYFP in Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP) larvae.
source: Using immunofluorescence, we verified that ChR2-EYFP is exclusively expressed in Hcrt neurons, and that all Hcrt neurons express ChR2-EYFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 40% of Hcrt neurons in Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP) larvae expressed c-fos after blue light exposure.
source: We observed that 40% of Hcrt neurons in Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP) larvae expressed c-fos, compared to only 5% of Hcrt neurons in control Tg(hcrt:EGFP) larvae (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Only 5% of Hcrt neurons in control Tg(hcrt:EGFP) larvae expressed c-fos after blue light exposure.
source: We observed that 40% of Hcrt neurons in Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP) larvae expressed c-fos, compared to only 5% of Hcrt neurons in control Tg(hcrt:EGFP) larvae (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The light paradigm employed activates Hcrt neurons.
source: This result confirms that the light paradigm employed activates Hcrt neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that c-fos expression is increased in Hcrt neurons after blue light exposure in Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP) larvae.

claim: Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP) larvae and their non-transgenic siblings exhibited similar levels of locomotor activity when illuminated with red light.
source: Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP) larvae and their non-transgenic siblings exhibited similar levels of locomotor activity when illuminated with red light (Figure 5C,D), a treatment that does not activate ChR2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: When illuminated with blue light the total locomotor activity of Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP) larvae increased by 46% compared to non-transgenic siblings.
source: In contrast, when illuminated with blue light the total locomotor activity of Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP) larvae increased by 46% compared to non-transgenic siblings (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP) larvae displayed a 25% increase in the maximum activity level reached during stimulation.
source: Specifically Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP) larvae displayed a 25% increase in the maximum activity level reached during stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP) larvae reached maximum activity level 20% faster than sibling controls.
source: Specifically Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP) larvae displayed a 25% increase in the maximum activity level reached during stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and reached this maximum activity level 20% faster (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) than sibling controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: hcrtr−/− larvae in the absence of the hcrt:ChR2-EYFP transgene respond to blue light in a manner similar to their hcrtr+/− and hcrtr+/+ siblings.
source: We first confirmed that hcrtr−/− larvae in the absence of the hcrt:ChR2-EYFP transgene respond to blue light in a manner similar to their hcrtr+/− and hcrtr+/+ siblings. Indeed, we observed no significant difference in the locomotor activity of larvae of the three genotypes during exposure to blue light (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP);hcrtr−/− larvae were 25% less active than their Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP);hcrtr+/− and Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP);hcrtr+/+ siblings in response to blue light.
source: However, Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP);hcrtr−/− larvae were 25% less active than their Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP);hcrtr+/− and Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP);hcrtr+/+ siblings in response to blue light.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic experiments.

claim: A functional hcrtr is important for Hcrt neuron-induced arousal.
source: This result indicates that a functional hcrtr is important for Hcrt neuron-induced arousal (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that hcrtr−/− larvae show reduced locomotor activity in response to Hcrt neuron stimulation.

claim: Mammalian and zebrafish Hcrt neurons coexpress other neurotransmitters and neuropeptides, such as glutamate and dynorphin.
source: Mammalian and zebrafish Hcrt neurons coexpress other neurotransmitters and neuropeptides, such as glutamate and dynorphin (Chou et al., 2001; Rosin et al., 2003; Appelbaum et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most, but not all, of the effect of stimulating Hcrt neurons on locomotor activity is due to Hcrt signaling.
source: These results suggest that most, but not all, of the effect of stimulating Hcrt neurons on locomotor activity is due to Hcrt signaling, similar to results obtained in mammals (Adamantidis et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of locomotor activity in different genotypes after Hcrt neuron stimulation.

claim: Optogenetic activation of only ∼8 larval zebrafish Hcrt neurons increases locomotor activity.
source: Thus, similar to Hcrt overexpression (Prober et al., 2006), optogenetic activation of only ∼8 larval zebrafish Hcrt neurons (an average of 40% of the 20 Hcrt neurons are c-fos positive upon stimulation with ChR2; Figure 5B) increases locomotor activity, consistent with a role for Hcrt neurons in promoting arousal (Lee et al., 2005; Mileykovskiy et al., 2005; Adamantidis et al., 2007; Carter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior literature.

claim: The effect of Hcrt neuron activation on locomotor activity appears to be significantly stronger in zebrafish than in mice.
source: This effect appears to be significantly stronger than the phenotype described in mice (Adamantidis et al., 2007; Carter et al., 2012), suggesting that zebrafish may be more sensitive to the arousing effect of Hcrt.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison with prior studies in mice.

claim: Zebrafish may be more sensitive to the arousing effect of Hcrt than mice.
source: This effect appears to be significantly stronger than the phenotype described in mice (Adamantidis et al., 2007; Carter et al., 2012), suggesting that zebrafish may be more sensitive to the arousing effect of Hcrt.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on comparison with prior studies in mice.

claim: Stimulation of Hcrt neurons results in activation of the LC in zebrafish larvae.
source: Indeed, over multiple trials in several animals we observed a significant increase in GCaMP6s fluorescence in Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP) larvae, but not in Tg(hcrt:EGFP) larvae (Figure 7B–E, Videos 1 and 2), indicating that stimulation of Hcrt neurons results in activation of the LC in zebrafish larvae.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging shown in Figure 7B–E.

claim: dbh−/− larvae were significantly less active during the 30 min of baseline recording than sibling controls.
source: As we previously observed (Figure 2D,E), dbh−/− larvae were significantly less active during the 30 min of baseline recording than sibling controls (dbh+/+ 31.0 ± 4.0, dbh+/− 39.7 ± 4.1 and dbh−/− 15.7 ± 2.6 s of activity, p < 0.05 by one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from baseline activity measurements.

claim: dbh−/− larvae were 25% less responsive to blue light than both dbh+/+ and dbh+/− larvae.
source: dbh−/− larvae were also 25% less responsive to blue light than both dbh+/+ and dbh+/− larvae (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: The ChR2-induced increase in locomotor activity was reduced by 76% in Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP);dbh−/− larvae compared to both Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP);dbh+/+ and Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP);dbh+/− siblings.
source: However, when Hcrt neurons were activated optogenetically the requirement for NE became more pronounced, as the ChR2-induced increase in locomotor activity was reduced by 76% in Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP);dbh−/− larvae compared to both Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP);dbh+/+ and Tg(hcrt:ChR2-EYFP);dbh+/− siblings (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: NE is an important effector of Hcrt-neuron induced arousal.
source: Thus, while it is possible that supranormal optogenetic activation of Hcrt neurons could make NE more important for Hcrt-induced locomotor activity than it is under normal conditions, these results suggest that NE is an important effector of Hcrt-neuron induced arousal.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that NE is required for most of the locomotor activity induced by Hcrt neuron stimulation.

claim: NE was the first catecholamine to be identified as a neurotransmitter by Ulf von Euler in 1946.
source: The first catecholamine to be identified as a neurotransmitter by Ulf von Euler in 1946, NE has been implicated in many aspects of physiology and behavior (Berridge and Waterhouse, 2003; Weinshenker and Schroeder, 2007; Sara, 2009).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge and citations to prior literature.

claim: Exogenous NE is a potent arousal-promoting agent.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate that exogenous NE is a potent arousal-promoting agent (reviewed in Berridge et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: In Drosophila, lack of endogenous octopamine results in increased sleep.
source: In Drosophila, lack of endogenous octopamine, which is considered the invertebrate equivalent of NE, results in increased sleep (Crocker and Sehgal, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Only 10% of dbh−/− pups produced by dbh+/− mothers survive embryonic development in mice.
source: However, only 10% of dbh−/− pups produced by dbh+/− mothers survive embryonic development and no dbh−/− pups are born to dbh−/− mothers; all such embryos die by embryonic day 13.5 (Thomas et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: All dbh−/− embryos from dbh−/− mothers die by embryonic day 13.5 in mice.
source: However, only 10% of dbh−/− pups produced by dbh+/− mothers survive embryonic development and no dbh−/− pups are born to dbh−/− mothers; all such embryos die by embryonic day 13.5 (Thomas et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The embryonic lethality in dbh mutant mice was hypothesized to be due to abnormal heart development or function.
source: Although the basis of the embryonic lethality is unclear, it was hypothesized to be due to abnormal heart development or function, as the hearts of mutant embryos display greater heterogeneity in cell size and orientation (Thomas et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Supplementation of drinking water during gestation with dihydroxyphenylserine (DOPS) rescues the embryonic lethal phenotype in dbh mutant mice.
source: Supplementation of drinking water during gestation with dihydroxyphenylserine (DOPS), which is converted to NE by L-aromatic-amino-acid decarboxylase (AADC), rescues the embryonic lethal phenotype.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about dbh mutant mice.

claim: Following birth, DOPS supplementation is not required for continued survival of dbh−/− pups in mice.
source: Following birth, DOPS supplementation is not required for continued survival of dbh−/− pups.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about dbh mutant mice.

claim: dbh−/− mice that reach adulthood were initially reported as having normal sleep/wake cycles.
source: Surprisingly, dbh−/− mice that reach adulthood were initially reported as having normal sleep/wake cycles (Hunsley and Palmiter, 2003), although a later study reported a 20% increase in sleep (Ouyang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A later study reported a 20% increase in sleep in dbh−/− mice.
source: Surprisingly, dbh−/− mice that reach adulthood were initially reported as having normal sleep/wake cycles (Hunsley and Palmiter, 2003), although a later study reported a 20% increase in sleep (Ouyang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Mice lacking dbh exhibit higher levels of dopamine.
source: These contradictory results could arise from differences in methodology, a relatively subtle and thus poorly reproducible sleep phenotype, or the complication that mice lacking dbh also exhibit higher levels of dopamine, the substrate of DBH and a major neurotransmitter in the brain.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the biochemical consequences of dbh mutation.

claim: Sleep can be distinguished from inactivity using electrophysiology or three behavioral criteria.
source: Sleep can be distinguished from inactivity using electrophysiology or three behavioral criteria (Campbell and Tobler, 1984; Borbely and Tobler, 1996; Allada and Siegel, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Sleep primarily occurs during specific periods of the circadian cycle.
source: First, sleep primarily occurs during specific periods of the circadian cycle.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about sleep.

claim: Animals exhibit an increased arousal threshold during sleep.
source: Second, animals exhibit an increased arousal threshold during sleep, although they can still be aroused by strong stimuli, thus distinguishing sleep from paralysis or coma.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about sleep.

claim: Sleep is controlled by a homeostatic system.
source: Third, sleep is controlled by a homeostatic system, which can be demonstrated as an increased need for sleep following sleep deprivation.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about sleep.

claim: Rest in zebrafish meets the behavioral definition of sleep.
source: Based on these criteria, it has been shown that rest in a variety of organisms, including zebrafish (Zhdanova et al., 2001; Prober et al., 2006; Yokogawa et al., 2007), meets the behavioral definition of sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Several groups have demonstrated behavioral, anatomical, genetic and pharmacological conservation of sleep between zebrafish and mammals.
source: Several groups have demonstrated behavioral, anatomical, genetic and pharmacological conservation of sleep between zebrafish and mammals, establishing zebrafish as a simple vertebrate model for sleep research (Zhdanova et al., 2001; Kaslin et al., 2004; Faraco et al., 2006; Prober et al., 2006; Renier et al., 2007; Yokogawa et al., 2007; Rihel et al., 2010; Gandhi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Prazosin most faithfully phenocopied the dbh sleep/wake phenotype among the drugs tested.
source: Among these drugs, prazosin most faithfully phenocopied the dbh sleep/wake phenotype (reduced day and night activity and increased day and night sleep) with differences observed in sleep bout number.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of the effects of different drugs on sleep/wake behavior.

claim: Clonidine reduced activity and increased sleep during the day, but had almost no effect at night.
source: Clonidine reduced activity and increased sleep during the day, but had almost no effect at night.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological experiments.

claim: Bopindolol increased sleep during the day and night, but only inhibited activity at night.
source: Bopindolol increased sleep during the day and night, but only inhibited activity at night.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological experiments.

claim: Alpha1-adrenergic receptors could be the main facilitators of noradrenergic modulation of larval zebrafish sleep.
source: These observations suggest that alpha1-adrenergic receptors could be the main facilitators of noradrenergic modulation of larval zebrafish sleep.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that prazosin most faithfully phenocopies the dbh mutant.

claim: Chronic loss of NE in dbh mutant mice may induce compensatory mechanisms during development that do not occur in response to chronic loss of NE in zebrafish.
source: One possible explanation is that the chronic loss of NE in dbh mutant mice may induce compensatory mechanisms during development that do not occur in response to chronic loss of NE in zebrafish.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposed as a possible explanation for differences between mice and zebrafish.

claim: DOPS treatment during gestation may affect developmental processes that ultimately affect behavior in dbh mutant mice.
source: Another possibility is that DOPS treatment during gestation affects developmental processes that ultimately affect behavior.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposed as a possible explanation for differences between mice and zebrafish.

claim: BAT thermogenesis has been shown to promote slow wave sleep.
source: BAT thermogenesis has been shown to promote slow wave sleep (Dewasmes et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: BAT thermogenesis is required for sleep rebound after sleep deprivation.
source: BAT thermogenesis has been shown to promote slow wave sleep (Dewasmes et al., 2003) and to be required for sleep rebound after sleep deprivation (Szentirmai and Kapas, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Genetic ablation of dbh could induce two competing effects in mice: reduced BAT thermogenesis in the periphery (inhibiting sleep) and interference with LC arousal function in the CNS (inhibiting wakefulness).
source: Therefore, genetic ablation of dbh could induce two competing effects. In the periphery, lack of NE reduces BAT thermogenesis and thus inhibits sleep. In the central nervous system, lack of NE interferes with the normal arousal function of the LC and thus inhibits wakefulness.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposed as a possible explanation for the minor sleep phenotype in dbh mutant mice.

claim: The combination of reduced BAT thermogenesis and interference with LC arousal function could result in a minor sleep increase in dbh−/− mice.
source: The combination of these two opposing forces could result in a minor sleep increase in dbh−/− mice, and the magnitude of this phenotype might be particularly sensitive to experimental conditions.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposed as a possible explanation for the minor sleep phenotype in dbh mutant mice.

claim: Zebrafish larvae and flies do not regulate their body temperature.
source: However, zebrafish larvae and flies do not regulate their body temperature and are thus subject only to the sleep promoting effects of NE ablation, resulting in a dramatic increase in sleep.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about zebrafish and fly physiology.

claim: Lack of beta-adrenergic receptor signaling potentiates responses to sensory stimuli.
source: Furthermore, the inability of prazosin (which increases sleep during day and night) or clonidine (which increases sleep during the day) to recapitulate the phenotype suggests that the observed reduction in arousal threshold is not simply a consequence of lighter sleep due to 'over-sleeping' in the dbh mutant. These observations suggest that lack of beta-adrenergic receptor signaling potentiates responses to sensory stimuli
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that bopindolol, but not prazosin or clonidine, reduces arousal threshold.

claim: NE reuptake inhibitors such as atomoxetine are used to treat patients suffering from Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD).
source: and are particularly interesting considering that NE reuptake inhibitors such as atomoxetine, which increase NE signaling, are used to treat patients suffering from Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) (Garnock-Jones and Keating, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Dopamine agonists have been shown to increase locomotion in zebrafish larvae.
source: Furthermore, dopamine agonists have been shown to increase locomotion in zebrafish larvae (Rihel et al., 2010; Irons et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dopamine promotes locomotor development in zebrafish larvae.
source: and dopamine promotes locomotor development in zebrafish larvae (Lambert et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Dopaminergic stimulation during anesthesia produces a robust arousal response.
source: This hypothesis is supported by zebrafish studies implicating dopamine in arousal modulation (Burgess and Granato, 2007; Mu et al., 2012) as well as work demonstrating that dopaminergic stimulation during anesthesia produces a robust arousal response (Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Zebrafish studies implicate dopamine in arousal modulation.
source: This hypothesis is supported by zebrafish studies implicating dopamine in arousal modulation (Burgess and Granato, 2007; Mu et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In humans, Hcrt neurons are reciprocally connected to other important arousal centers such as the cholinergic basal forebrain, the histaminergic tuberomammillary nucleus, the dopaminergic ventral tegmental area and the serotonergic dorsal raphe.
source: Furthermore, in humans, Hcrt neurons are reciprocally connected to other important arousal centers such as the cholinergic basal forebrain, the histaminergic tuberomammillary nucleus, the dopaminergic ventral tegmental area and the serotonergic dorsal raphe (Alexandre et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Many of the connections between Hcrt neurons and other arousal centers present in humans are also present in zebrafish.
source: Many of these connections are also present in zebrafish, with Hcrt neurons projecting to dopaminergic, histaminergic and serotonergic populations (Panula et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Endogenous NE is required to maintain normal levels of wakefulness in a diurnal vertebrate.
source: In summary, we have demonstrated that endogenous NE is required to maintain normal levels of wakefulness in a diurnal vertebrate.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: This study, together with previous reports in Drosophila and mice, support a phylogenetically conserved role for endogenous NE in promoting wakefulness.
source: This study, together with previous reports in Drosophila (Crocker and Sehgal, 2008) and mice (Ouyang et al., 2004), support a phylogenetically conserved role for endogenous NE in promoting wakefulness.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the current study and citations to prior literature.

claim: The zebrafish dbh mutant is a useful tool for studying processes that are thought to involve NE, including the fight-or-flight response, congestive heart failure, cognitive disorders such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, and neuropsychiatric disorders including depression and ADHD.
source: Finally, we established and characterized the zebrafish dbh mutant, a useful tool for studying other processes that are thought to involve NE, including the fight-or-flight response (Colwill and Creton, 2011), congestive heart failure (Thomas and Marks, 1978), cognitive disorders such as Alzheimer's (Chalermpalanupap et al., 2013) and Parkinson's diseases (Rommelfanger et al., 2007), and neuropsychiatric disorders including depression and ADHD (Chamberlain and Robbins, 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on the characterization of the dbh mutant in this study and citations to prior literature about NE's role in various processes.

claim: Larvae were exposed to 100 µM prazosin.
source: We found that, compared to larvae exposed to dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) vehicle alone, larvae exposed to 100 µM prazosin showed lower overall activity (Figure 1A,D) and activity when awake (Figure 1B,E) during both day and night
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data describing the methods and results.

claim: Larvae exposed to 100 µM prazosin showed lower overall activity during both day and night compared to DMSO controls.
source: We found that, compared to larvae exposed to dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) vehicle alone, larvae exposed to 100 µM prazosin showed lower overall activity (Figure 1A,D) and activity when awake (Figure 1B,E) during both day and night
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,D.

claim: Larvae exposed to 100 µM prazosin showed lower activity when awake during both day and night compared to DMSO controls.
source: We found that, compared to larvae exposed to dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) vehicle alone, larvae exposed to 100 µM prazosin showed lower overall activity (Figure 1A,D) and activity when awake (Figure 1B,E) during both day and night
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,E.

claim: Larvae exposed to 100 µM prazosin showed an increase in sleep during both day (+140%) and night (+60%).
source: as well as an increase in sleep during both day (+140%) and night (+60%) (Figure 1C,F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The increase in sleep in prazosin-treated larvae was primarily due to an increase in the number of sleep bouts (+110% during the day and +70% during the night).
source: This increase in sleep was primarily due to an increase in the number of sleep bouts (+110% during the day and +70% during the night, Figure 1G)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Prazosin-treated larvae showed a smaller increase in sleep bout duration (+20% during the day).
source: as well as a smaller increase in sleep bout duration (+20% during the day) (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: A 23% reduction in sleep latency at night was observed in prazosin-treated animals.
source: We also observed a 23% reduction in sleep latency at night in prazosin-treated animals (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The dbh mutant allele contains a four nucleotide insertion in the third exon.
source: The dbh mutant allele that we generated contains a four nucleotide insertion in the third exon, which gives rise to a premature stop codon, resulting in a predicted 178 amino acid peptide lacking the DBH active site, instead of the full length 614 amino acid protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The dbh mutant allele gives rise to a premature stop codon.
source: The dbh mutant allele that we generated contains a four nucleotide insertion in the third exon, which gives rise to a premature stop codon, resulting in a predicted 178 amino acid peptide lacking the DBH active site, instead of the full length 614 amino acid protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The dbh mutant allele results in a predicted 178 amino acid peptide lacking the DBH active site.
source: The dbh mutant allele that we generated contains a four nucleotide insertion in the third exon, which gives rise to a premature stop codon, resulting in a predicted 178 amino acid peptide lacking the DBH active site, instead of the full length 614 amino acid protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The full length DBH protein is 614 amino acids.
source: The dbh mutant allele that we generated contains a four nucleotide insertion in the third exon, which gives rise to a premature stop codon, resulting in a predicted 178 amino acid peptide lacking the DBH active site, instead of the full length 614 amino acid protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Adult dbh−/− fish often die following anesthesia with tricaine at a commonly used dose (0.16 mg/ml).
source: During the course of routine genotyping by fin clipping, we found that adult dbh−/− fish often die following anesthesia with tricaine (E10521, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, United States) at a commonly used dose (0.16 mg/ml).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations during routine procedures.

claim: A lower concentration of tricaine (0.08 mg/ml) allowed survival of dbh−/− fish.
source: A lower concentration of tricaine (0.08 mg/ml) allowed survival of dbh−/− fish.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations during routine procedures.

claim: dbh−/− fish sometimes died during or shortly after mating.
source: Furthermore, dbh−/− fish sometimes died during or shortly after mating, perhaps due to a heightened sensitivity to stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: dbh−/− larvae respond normally to sensory stimuli such as gentle poking.
source: dbh−/− larvae respond normally to sensory stimuli such as gentle poking.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.
